transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-11-27 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~42m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lara Chen (Cascade Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Platform), Amir Khatib (CTO)

Summary (auto): Redwood walked through Optimize batching and KV/prefix cache recommendations and a cost model. Discussed hit-rate assumptions, memory tradeoffs, and dedicated vs hosted options. Action items and pricing follow-up.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, good to meet you. quick intro - im maya, im on the AE team at Redwood, with diego our solutions engineer. how's the sound?
[00:12] Lara: good yes, can hear you.
[00:15] Diego: hi all, i'll drive the technical part, we'll go through some numbers and a short demo of the Optimize console and the batching/kv cache settings.
[00:28] Maya: our goal for today is to share the recommendation for your chat workload - prefix cache hit assumptions, batching configs, and the cost model we used to estimate per-session token spend. then we can map to your SLOs and pilot timeline.
[00:40] Tom: sounds good. we want to see where we can get token costs down without blowing up tail latency. our SLAs are 200-300ms p95 for user-facing chat.
[00:52] Diego: great, i'll start with batching. so Redwood supports continuous batching which accumulates in-flight requests up to a latency budget; with our runtime we try to maximize GPU utilization while honoring latency SLOs. in the console you can tweak the max-wait and soft-deadline.
[01:10] Lara: when you say "max-wait" is that per request or per batch?
[01:14] Diego: it's the window we hold the request to try and form a larger batch. so if you set max-wait to 15ms we'll hold for up to 15ms before dispatching. we also have a small per-batch token folding optimisation that helps with long contexts.
[01:28] Amir: and how does that interact with our p95 requirement? if we wait we might increase p95, right?
[01:33] Diego: correct - it's a tradeoff. our cost model shows diminishing returns after about 20-30ms wait for your traffic shape. For conversational workloads with many short turns, batching at ~10-15ms often yields 20-30% token-cost reduction while keeping p95 within 10-20ms of baseline.
[01:52] Tom: interesting. what's the baseline - hosted or dedicated?
[01:55] Maya: baseline in the slides is hosted Redwood API latencies. for dedicated capacity we can tune the batch sizing more aggressively because you control the throughput. we included both in the spreadsheet.
[02:08] Diego: next i want to show prefix/KV cache - this is where we see the biggest wins for multi-turn chat. we cache the model KV states for prefixes (stable system prompts + recent history) to avoid re-computing the prefix tokens every request.
[02:22] Lara: is that stored per-session? what's the memory cost?
[02:26] Diego: it's per-session or per-conversation-key depending on your routing. memory is the main tradeoff; the cost model has two lines: expected hit-rate and average prefix size. e.g., at 70% hit-rate and average prefix 350 tokens, you can cut about 40-60% of redundant compute on prefix tokens.
[02:44] Lara: our typical prompt with metadata is closer to 400-600 tokens. we also sometimes insert user profile vectors in the prompt, so prefixes vary a lot.
[02:53] Diego: that's fine - the cache can be configured to evict based on total cached bytes or LRU. also we offer partial prefix caching (cache only top-k attention blocks) for very large prefixes to reduce memory. that's in the Optimize console under "KV cache policy - partial caching".
[03:10] Tom: and for cost model inputs you need hit-rate and prefix length distribution?
[03:13] Diego: yes, hit-rate, avg prefix tokens, frequency of cold sessions, quantization level (int8 vs int4), and whether you use dedicated GPUs.
[03:23] Amir: question on quantization - if we move to int4 to reduce memory, do we see any latency regressions?
[03:28] Diego: typically int4 reduces memory and can slightly reduce latency on some kernels, but there are model-accuracy tradeoffs. we can recommend per-model quant profiles in the Optimize report; we show expected delta on throughput/latency and a quality-safety metric derived from evals you provide.
[03:44] Lara: okay. can you walk through the spreadsheet example you prepared?
[03:48] Maya: sure, diego i think you had the cost model open?
[03:51] Diego: yes. so here's the simplified row: baseline tokens per session 1200, prefix tokens 400, dynamic tokens 800. with no cache and no batching, cost per session X. with batching at 15ms and prefix cache at 70% hit-rate, you reduce compute tokens by ~350 tokens per session which translates to ~35% cost reduction in the model compute line. further gains if you put on dedicated GPUs with higher density.
[04:20] Tom: these numbers assume the same model, right? if we switch to a cheaper open model with similar quality, that changes everything.
[04:27] Maya: yes, model choice is a big lever - the spreadsheet has toggles for model family (open vs Llama-family vs Redwood-verified optimized variants). part of Optimize is recommending the best model + quant configuration for your workload.
[04:39] [05:00] Diego: demo time - i'll share my screen, jumping into the console, quick overview: Optimize tab, batching controls, KV cache policy, per-route expected savings. (screen share noises)
[05:15] [05:30] Diego: here you can see a live simulation: feed in your traffic histogram and it will simulate expected batch sizes, GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens. we also show p95 delta so you can tune for cost vs latency.
[05:45] Lara: can we upload our traffic histogram?
[05:48] Diego: yes, you can upload a CSV with inter-arrival times, token distribution, and session IDs - we used a sanitized sample from Cascade for these numbers.
[06:00] Tom: how accurate are hit-rate estimates? if our bot uses personalization, hit-rates might be lower.
[06:06] Diego: accuracy depends on how representative the sample is. we run tracer analysis on session keys and prefix similarity; for highly personalized prompts we suggest a smaller prefix cache and rely more on batching. we also provide a conservative and optimistic projection in the sheet.
[06:22] Lara: security question: for KV cache state, is the cached state encrypted at rest? who owns the keys?
[06:28] Diego: good question - for hosted API cached states are encrypted at rest with our KMS; for Private/VPC deployments you manage the KMS/HSM and keys. we also log access to the cache in audit logs for SOC 2 and ISO requirements.
[06:45] Amir: and what about data residency? some sessions must remain in EU region.
[06:49] Maya: we can route by region - Smart routing policies can keep EU traffic in EU endpoints or fall back to a compatible variant when capacity shifts. Dedicated and Private give more control here.
[07:00] Tom: what about fallback behavior - if cache miss spike causes more load do you auto-scale?
[07:05] Diego: yes, autoscaling and burst capacity are configurable. we have soft and hard limits to protect your budget; plus our runtime will route to lower-cost model variants when SLA allows.
[07:18] Lara: any gotchas on cold starts and cache warm-up for a pilot?
[07:21] Diego: you'll see a warm-up period - recommended to pre-warm by replaying recent sessions for the pilot or seeding cache with top-k prefixes. we can help with a warm-up script as part of the pilot.
[07:33] Tom: ok, about dedicated - what's the typical commit needed to get the density that makes batching and caching pay off?
[07:40] Maya: it depends on throughput; our sales handbook maps expected QPS to GPU pool sizes. for many customers, meaningful unit-cost improvement appears at sustained QPS that justifies a monthly reserved capacity - spreadsheet has a breakpoint chart.
[07:53] Amir: competitors - we've looked at Vertex and a Triton self-host path, what are the main differences?
[07:58] Diego: Vertex provides managed endpoints but lacks the deep Optimize tooling (the batching+prefix simulation and per-route cost model). Triton self-host gives control but requires building the orchestration, autoscaling, and cache infra; Redwood bundles runtime + Optimize + routing with commercial SLAs.
[08:15] Lara: ok. on compliance, we need SOC 2 plus ability to integrate with our audit pipeline. is Redwood's audit log schema compatible?
[08:22] Maya: yes we have an audit log export format (JSON lines) and prebuilt connectors to Splunk/Datadog. we'll share the security pack.
[08:30] Diego: quick note - for very latency-sensitive routes you can set no-batching and no-cache (cold path) while optimizing background/async routes heavily. that's a common pattern.
[08:42] Tom: we have some async ingestion jobs that could benefit.
[08:45] Maya: per-route controls in the console let you assign policies per endpoint.
[08:50] [09:00] Diego: walking through a concrete example: assume 1k sessions/hour, avg tokens per session 1.2k, average prefix 450. with 70% prefix hit and batching 15ms we get approx 38% cost reduction in compute compared to baseline hosted. switching to dedicated GPUs gives an additional ~10-15% reduction but requires commit.
[09:24] Lara: if we choose to pilot, what telemetry will you need from us?
[09:28] Diego: sample traffic histogram CSV, a representative test dataset, and a small API key or VPC peering for the benchmark. we'll keep any PII out - we request synthetic/sanitized samples for initial run.
[09:40] Tom: we can do that.
[09:42] [10:00] Maya: quick objection handling - you might be worried about vendor lock and model portability. with Redwood you can pin model versions and we support exporting cached artifacts if you run private. also we provide rollout policies and can fall back to a model variant.
[10:15] Amir: what's the SLA for the dedicated offering?
[10:18] Maya: we provide SLA-backed uptime and latency targets in Dedicated contracts and enhanced support during pilots. we'll attach the SLA doc.
[10:24] Lara: governance - can we limit who can change caching policy?
[10:28] Diego: yes RBAC is integrated in the console; changes are audited.
[10:32] [12:00] Diego: quick demo wrap - here's the per-route dashboard showing token-level cost breakdown, cache hit rate chart over time, and recommended quant profile. (screen -> small lag)
[12:18] Tom: the hit-rate chart you showed - is that simulated or from live data?
[12:22] Diego: in the demo it's simulated using your histogram but we can run a short live capture if you give us a test key.
[12:30] Lara: i'd like to see a live run.
[12:33] Maya: we'll include that in the benchmark action - diego will run a 1-hour test and share the logs.
[12:40] [26:00] (several minutes of Q&A about implementation details - session key hashing, eviction policies, and memory sizing; some back-and-forth about large user profiles causing lower cache hit rates)
[26:30] Diego: on eviction we recommend LRU with a TTL for session inactivity; critical sessions can be pinned for VIP customers. also when you have user-profile heavy prompts we suggest hybrid: small prefix cache + more aggressive batching.
[27:00] Lara: do you provide a preview of prefix states so we can audit what's cached?
[27:05] Diego: yes for Private deployments we can enable a debug view; for hosted we redact PII and provide hashed previews and statistics.
[27:16] Tom: about cost ceilings - can we set soft budget caps per-route?
[27:20] Maya: yes, the console supports budget policies and will alert and optionally throttle or route to cheaper model variants when thresholds hit.
[27:30] Amir: this looks promising. what's the recommended timeline for a pilot?
[27:33] Maya: typically 2-4 weeks for initial benchmark and pilot config, then 8-12 weeks for a production rollout depending on scope. we suggested a pilot kickoff week of 2027-12-06.
[27:45] Lara: sounds good.
[27:47] [35:00] Final recap: Maya: recap - we'll send pricing + cost model spreadsheet, diego runs 1-hour benchmark with your test key, tom will provide dataset and SSO contact, we aim to kick off pilot week of 12/06. any other items?
[35:20] Tom: please include security pack and SLA docs.
[35:25] Maya: will do.
[35:30] Amir: thanks everyone.
[35:32] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up via email with links and next steps.

END TRANSCRIPT
